structured_output.hypothesis: If the claim holds, the height-velocity curves of boys and girls aged about 5–19 y have nearly the same shape once one is shifted in time, and the girls' adolescent acceleration begins, peaks and ends earlier than the boys'.
structured_output.pass_criterion: All of the following hold. (1) The age at peak height velocity is earlier in girls than in boys by at least 1.0 y. (2) The age of the pre-pubertal velocity minimum (onset of acceleration) is earlier in girls by at least 0.5 y. (3) The age at which velocity falls back to within 1 cm/yr of its late-adolescent floor (end of acceleration) is earlier in girls by at least 0.5 y. (4) After shifting the girls' curve by the best-fitting lag (searched over -3 to +3 y), the Pearson correlation between the two velocity curves is at least 0.90. (5) Peak velocities differ by at least 5% (an amplitude difference exists).
structured_output.fail_criterion: Any one of the following refutes the claim. (a) The girls' peak-velocity age is earlier by less than 0.5 y, or is not earlier. (b) The girls' onset or end of acceleration is not earlier than the boys'. (c) The best-lag correlation between the curves is below 0.80, meaning the shapes are not similar. (d) Peak velocities differ by less than 5%, so there is no amplitude difference.
structured_output.interpretation: 'Growth velocity' is annual height increment in cm/yr, computed by differencing the sex-specific median stature-for-age at 12-month intervals. This is the modern form of Thompson's curves of rate of growth. 'Phase' is the timing of the adolescent spurt: onset, peak and end. 'Amplitude' is peak velocity. 'Similar shape' is the best-lag correlation. Modern reinterpretation: the data are cross-sectional smoothed medians, not individual longitudinal series. Median-curve velocity therefore blurs individual peaks and underestimates peak height velocity, but the timing difference between the sexes should still show. The dataset has monthly medians for ages 61–228 months (5–19 y).

dataset.name: Growth reference data for 5-19 years (WHO 2007), height-for-age
dataset.why_it_fits: It provides downloadable tables of height-for-age (L, M, S and percentiles) by sex and by month from 5 to 19 y. The M column (median stature) gives sex-specific median stature. Differencing it gives the velocity curves for each sex, from which peak, onset, end and amplitude can be measured.
